title: Kobalos Malware Investigation
description: You are an incident responder tasked with investigating a potential Kobalos malware infection in your organization's high-performance computing (HPC) environment. Kobalos is a sophisticated backdoor malware that targets HPC clusters and other high-profile systems. It provides remote access, terminal session capabilities, and credential stealing functionality. Your mission is to investigate the compromised systems, identify the malware's persistence mechanisms, and contain the threat. The scenario involves identifying suspicious services, persistence mechanisms, and lateral movement evidence.

levels.title: Introduction
levels.content:
You are an incident responder tasked with investigating a potential Kobalos malware infection in your organization's high-performance computing (HPC) environment. Kobalos is a sophisticated backdoor malware that targets HPC clusters and other high-profile systems. It provides remote access, terminal session capabilities, and credential stealing functionality.

Your mission is to investigate the compromised systems, identify the malware's persistence mechanisms, and contain the threat. The scenario involves identifying suspicious services, persistence mechanisms, and lateral movement evidence. Kobalos typically infiltrates systems through unauthorized services, maintains persistence via systemd configurations, and attempts lateral movement through file transfers and remote command execution. This scenario will guide you through the process of identifying and mitigating these threats in a controlled environment.

levels.title: Get Access
levels.cloud_content: Access the target host (IP: 192.168.50.5) via SSH using the provided credentials. Username: cyrano, Password: cyrano. Enter the word 'start' to progress to the next level.

levels.title: Suspicious Service Discovery
levels.content: While monitoring your organization's HPC environment, you noticed unusual network traffic originating from the target host. Your first task is to identify any unauthorized or suspicious services running on this host that might be responsible for this activity. Look for services that are not part of the standard system configuration or that have unusual properties. You are expected to find a text file named 'malicious-service' indicating the suspicious service.
levels.solution: Use standard Linux commands to list running services and check their legitimacy. Look for any services that are not part of the standard system configuration or that have unusual properties.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Understand that malicious services often deviate from standard system configurations.

hints.title: Directional Hint
hints.content: Use standard Linux commands to list running services and check their legitimacy.

hints.title: Near-Spoiler Hint
hints.content: Look for any services that are not part of the standard system configuration or that have unusual properties.

levels.title: Persistence Discovery
levels.content: Now that you've identified a suspicious service, you need to determine how it maintains persistence on the system. Investigate the system's startup mechanisms to find out how the service is automatically started after reboot. Look for systemd services, timers, and cron jobs that might be responsible for maintaining persistence. You are expected to find a text file named 'malicious-persistence' indicating the persistence mechanism.
levels.solution: Check systemd services and timers, as well as cron jobs, to identify how the suspicious service maintains persistence on the system.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Persistence mechanisms often involve system startup configurations.

hints.title: Near-Spoiler Hint
hints.content: Look for cron jobs that might be responsible for starting the suspicious service.

levels.title: Lateral Movement Investigation
levels.content: Your investigation has revealed that the malware might be attempting to move laterally within your network. Examine the system for evidence of file transfers or remote execution used to move between hosts. Focus on any connections to the next-target host (IP: 192.168.50.6). Look for evidence of lateral movement such as logs of file transfers or remote command execution. You are expected to find a text file named 'malicious-lateral-movement' indicating the lateral movement evidence.
levels.solution: Investigate systemd services, timers, and any scripts or binaries related to file transfers. Look for evidence of connections to the next-target host.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Lateral movement often involves file transfers or remote command execution.

hints.title: Near-Spoiler Hint
hints.content: Look for scripts or binaries related to file transfers.
